questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go to the US with the typical American college experience with campus, sports and so on. I wanted to go somehwere that has a great outdoors life and where I could go skiing. I was looking to have the perfect end for my university time and this fulfilled that dream.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was happy to hear that American universities were currently quite unpopular among Danish students, so my hopes were really high to get in and so I got my first priority as well.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I was flooded with welcome newsletters and so on from the American international office. It was a bit chaotic but after looking through everything you need, you will get a sense of what and when you have to do. Both international offices were quick to assist so there was always an answer. Shoutout to Pernille at this point.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I arrived 2 weeks before the scheduled international welcome day where I also swung by the university to collect my student card, and you could also ask questions there on the spot.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: They got a new head of exchange students counsellor now (Jessie), and he made it his mission to overhaul the whole websites and checklists of what you need to do and he seems to love his job so my guess is that it will only get better.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It's a bit tough but Americans are quite interested in having an international roommate I'd say. Many people reached out to me via Ralphie's List which is the university's internal housing website. You create a profile and then you can reach out to people or people reach out to you when you or they think you'd be a match. The only downside is that it is probably a bit harder to find someone who will take you for only a semester. I lived with two Americans in a classic house, and they took care of the lease and the leasing company which I was very grateful for.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: No exchange student lives on campus. On campus there are only dorms for freshmen (18 year olds). Everybody else lives around campus, in or around Boulder. Boulder is quite walkable and bikeable so it is easy to commute. Free buses and free e-bikes for all the students. The Hill is mostly only student houses and fraternities. I lived east of campus which is a bit quieter but just as close to campus. And all the other exchange students I've met also lived all relatively close to campus.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Exchange students also lived in Airbnbs and someone actually found housing through snapchat. Facebook groups work as well but I believe that Ralphie's List is the best. The sooner you start looking the better. I started looking at around the end of March I think and my roommate confirmed housing to me at the start of May. Finding housing for the spring semester is probably easier as there are less exchange students. We were around 150 and there are only about 50 coming in now.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very interesting to get more and more emails to set up their equivalents of KUnet and Canvas. Immediately you are a part of the 'herd' of the Colorado Buffaloes.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: At the mandatory international welcome day, registration occurs on campus with all the other international students, no matter if you're exchange or full time student. Before that, they tell you what to bring and what to expect and so on. It's all pretty smooth as long as you read every email and newsletter you get. At the end of the welcome event, you will be put in a room with all the other exchange students, this is where you have to look for people you think you will get along with. I was unlucky enough to sit at a table with people I had nothing in common with, so it was a challenge to get into other groups. You will find your people eventually, but these welcome events determine how soon you will find your people.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Boulder's international office ISSS is always very happy to help as they have probably heard every question you ask them already before.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got everything I wanted. As a master's student you have the choice to do either two graduate courses or 1 graduate course and 2 undergraduate courses. For the graduate class you actually need to have pre-requisites from their earlier classes from that maior, but I was told to just contact the head of that study department and she registered me into the graduate class that I wanted. For the undergraduate courses you just have to sign up as long as there as seats available.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I recommend doing 3 courses as you spend more time on campus and meet more people. Most classes are twice a week for 1h 15 mins each. If your Copenhagen schedule allows it, choose classes you would never get in CPH or Europe actually, they have very fun or specific classes. Learn something new and not something you have seen already 3 times before.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They have so many different faculties and programs with well respected professors and engaged lecturers. The only thing I wished for is that they would elaborate more on what to expect from a class, it's pretty hard to find out, as it is up to the teacher on how they want to design their class.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: One graduate class which was mixed with senior undergraduates. Two undergraduate classes from the first or second year. Freshman classes start with 100 until 400 for the senior classes. Graduate classes start at 500 until upwards. The higher the number, the more intensive the class. Lower classes are quite easy, of course it depends on the professors but it is mostly common sense and mediocere time management and then there is no way you will fail that class. Graduate classes are more work intensive, depending on the class you have a lot of homework or assignments.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Much more mandatory homework than from my experience in CPH. Again, it also depends on the teaching style from the professors. Some want to engage with the class, others will show more videos in their lectures as it is hard to engage with a class of 200 people. Most classes have 2 midterms and then a final. Some teachers put more emphasis on homework and less on exams. All in all I had a mix of midterms, homework, weekly quizzes, Canvas discussion assignments and cumulative exams.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
GEOG 2321: The Grography of Skiing and Snowboarding with Noah Molotch
GEOG 4712: Political Geography with John O'Loughlin
GEOG 5271: The Arctic Climate System with Mark Serreze

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
All of them. I looked up all the professors from my shortlist that I made on
ratemyprofessor.com
and there you can see what the professors and the courses are like. Serreze is the highest rated professor in the geography department and he is really an absolute legend. I am convinced that John O'Loughlin knows everything as he is also 78 years old, this was material wise my favorite course as I really learned a lot. Noah's class was quite easy as it is a sophomore class and he is just super passionate about going skiing. The class is low effort but quite nice and you get to tell people that you are studying skiing academically. This was the second time the class was offered as well so it is still a bit new but there were 200 people in that class who were eager to go skiing. (No you don't go skiing with the prof but he likes getting pictures from us in the powder.)

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Groceries are kind of the same price as DK depending on where you shop. I went out a lot, ate a lot, did a lot of trips. My most unexpected cost was probably a spontaenous trip to San Francisco as I unexpectely got tickets to Fred again. I was also very lucky and I could use a friend's car as she was not here for the semester so I also had to pay for driving around a bit. The most unexpected cost is the rent that I'm still paying as we couldn't find someone to take over my room.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Phone can be cheap but I still went with an unlimited Tmobile subscription for 50$. Eating out is quite expensive as you always have to consider the tips. If you're careful you can get really cheap flights. We went on a 9 night trip for Thanksgiving to Chicago, Miami and New Orleans and all the flights cost less than 300$. If you wanna go skiing, go for the Ikon Pass, as day passes at the resorts are stupidly expensive. I also took a 25 meals mealplan which cost around 250$. One entry to the dining hall will then be around 10$ and then you can stay there for as long as you want and eat as much as you can and want.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: This is what I was most excited about, as you can get involved in something you're good at or in something completely new.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
The student recreation center is the best thing that campus has to offer. You can play literally any sport you can think of, either by yourself, with friends or just random people. I played a lot of basketball, pickleball and squash. For 6$ you can rent ice hockey gear which I did with my roommates.
In the beginning of the semester there is a 'Be involved fair' where literally every club from the university has a stand and you can sign up for. I went to one rowing training but I had to stop as training times interfered with my class schedule. There is also a club for basically any sport, hobby, religion, ethnic group, study department and so on.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Make as much use of the recreation center as possible, it is a perfect example on where all their tuition money is flowing into. Go on hikes around Boulder, explore campus and the area. If you have American roommates, make them take you around and just tag along to anywhere. Accept every invitation you get no matter what it is for. Going out is super fun. As Boulder is not an enormous city, you will find your way around quite quickly and it will feel very homey.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go explore with people you meet or your roommates. I have done a roadtrip with my family before the exchange to Wyoming, Idaho and Utah with Yellowstone, the Grand Tetons and so on. I camped a night in the Great Sand Dunes with my roommate which was amazing. Roadtrips to Rocky Mountain National Park, visits to Denver. Rodeos are really fun! I have never seen so much sun continuously in my life, the weather is always good and we had high temperatures until November. We even saw the Northern Lights! Sadly this year was a late and warm ski season but as soon as it starts you can go skiing to Eldora, Arapahoe Basin, Copper Mountain etc. If you know you wanna go skiing, buy the pass as early as possible. Thanksgiving break we went to Chicago, Miami and New Orleans. I had one friend visit me where we went to New York as well. You will meet a ton of people and the spontaneous trips are always the most fun. And try to see many of their sports teams, the sports culture is amazing.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easiest thing I've ever done. Everybody is so welcoming. There may be many stereotypes and they might be true from time to time. The food scene is of course maybe a bit different, but I realized at some point that I will be okay with not eating the same stuff that I eat at home, so I fully indulged and tried to taste as many American foods as possible.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Don't sit in last row as there will be the students who don't wanna talk. Keep going back to the same spot for every class and boom you will have a buddy in class. Americans are the friendliest creatures and you will feel just like in a movie because it is exactly the same. However, a lot of them are scared to make friends with internationals as those will leave again pretty soon. The people who will be in the same shoes as you are all the other exchange students who are also looking for friends and it will be those that you will likely hang out with the most. As soon as you meet new international people, especially in the beginning, ask them to put you in any of their social media groups. In the beginning everybody just wants to be involved and not be alone. Everybody will always know someone else, so just tag along.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Travelling to the Southern states means they will have most likely a different political view. While I have had no bad experience with a Trump supporter, it is not difficult to identify them. Even though Colorado is quite advanced, recycling is basically inexistent. Car dependency is real, but your American friends are more than happy to drive you. Most Americans you meet are generally quite concerned about the current political situation and while I had no bad experience with it, it should not be forgotten. The Visa application was the most stressful part.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The genuine friendliness of the Americans. I appreciated the absence of annoying "Why are you going to the US" questions from back home, because the Americans are so happy you're there and every exchange student shares your enthusiasm. It is very easy to settle in when everybody speaks the same language. I most appreciated the sports culture, both as a fan and player.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1. Say yes to every invitation. 2. Make the most of the recreation center and campus. 3. Don't invite too many friends from home, it will prevent you from having the full experience.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't sign a year long lease and be friends with your roommates. Forget your European diet. Money will come back and kilos can be dropped. Boulder is btw the fittest city in the US.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Living the dream and making friends from all over the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Leaving and saying goodbye, which proves to me that it was worth it.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go live the dream, cowboys and cowgirls. I genuinely had fun writing this, I hope this helped and if this doesn't convince you, I don't know what will.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
